main.text: [III, 85] [col. 326] Chapter 29.
It is proved that חסידה hasida is the stork.

There is no need for long deliberation over which of so many interpretations of the word חסידה hasida should above all [col. 327] be chosen. For חסידה is certainly the stork. This is proved, first, from the name. For חסידה means pious and kind. And such is the stork. In Roman usage [says Ambrose ^{a)}] it is called the pious bird. And in Publius it is pietati-cultrix [cultivator of piety], in the very well-known verses quoted by Petronius:
The stork too, welcome, a wanderer, a guest, cultivator of piety, slender-footed, castanet-player.

The reason is obvious. It belongs to piety ἀμοιβὰς ἀποδιδόναι τοῖς προγόνοις [amoibas apodidonai tois progonois], to repay one's parents in turn, as Paul commands, 1 Tim. V, 4. And that the stork does this all writers testify with one voice. Among the older writers, consult on this matter Plato at the end of the first Alcibiades, and Aristotle, History of Animals, book 9, chapter 13, and Aristophanes in the Birds, where the jackdaw speaks thus,

Ἀλλ’ ἔστιν ἡμῖν τοῖσιν ὄρνισιν νόμος Παλαιὸς ἐν τοῖς τῶν πελαργῶν κύρβεσιν, Ἐπὴν ὁ πατὴρ ὁ πελαργὸς ἐκπετησίμους Πάντας ποιήσῃ τοὺς πελαργιδεῖς τρέφων, Δεῖ τοὺς νεοττοὺς τὸν πατέρα πάλιν τρέφειν. [All’ estin hēmin toisin ornisin nomos / Palaios en tois tōn pelargōn kyrbesin, / Epēn ho patēr ho pelargos ekpetēsimous / Pantas poiēsē tous pelargideis trephōn, / Dei tous neottous ton patera palin trephein.]

But for us birds there is an ancient law in the tables of the storks: that after the father stork, by feeding them, has made all the chicks able to fly, they in turn must feed their father. Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 23: They in turn rear their mothers in old age. And Solinus: They have remarkable piety. For as much time as they have spent rearing their young, for so long are they in turn fed by their own chicks. And Aelian, book 3, chapter 23: Τρέφειν μὲν τοὺς πατέρας πελαγοὶ γεγηρακότας καὶ ἐθέλουσι, καὶ ἐμελέτησαν. κελεύει δ’ αὐτοὺς νόμος ἀνθρωπικὸς οὐδὲ εἰς τοῦτο, ἀλλ’ αἰτία τούτων φύσις ἀγαθή [Trephein men tous pateras pelagoi gegērakotas kai ethelousi, kai emeletēsan. keleuei d’ autous nomos anthrōpikos oude eis touto, all’ aitia toutōn physis agathē]. Storks are willing and eager to feed their fathers when they are old. Not that any human law compels them to it; rather, the goodness of nature is the cause. Therefore, when Croesus asked the Seven Sages, Τί τῶν ζώων εὐδαιμονέστατον; [Ti tōn zōōn eudaimonestaton?] Which animal was the happiest?, some answered Πελαργούς [Pelargous], storks, because δίχα νόμου τῇ φύσει τὸ δίκαιον ἔχουσι [dicha nomou tē physei to dikaion echousi], they observe justice by nature and without law. So Apostolius, Proverb 1141. And in Origen, Against Celsus, book 4, Celsus asserts that for this very reason εὐσεβεστέρους εἶναι τοὺς πελαργοὺς [III, 86] τῶν ἀνθρώπων [eusebesterous einai tous pelargous tōn anthrōpōn], storks are more pious than men. And Aelian, book 10, chapter 16: Αἰγύπτιοι τοὺς πελαργοὺς καὶ προσκυνοῦσιν, ἐπεὶ τοὺς πατέρας γηροκομοῦσιν [Aigyptioi tous pelargous kai proskynousin, epei tous pateras gērokomousin], the Egyptians worship storks, because they feed their parents in old age. And in the Hieroglyphics of Horus, book 2, chapter 55: Φιλοπάτορα βουλόμενοι σημῆναι ἄνθρωπον, πελαργὸν ζωγραφοῦσιν· ὑπὸ γὰρ τῶν γεννησάντων ἐκτραφεὶς οὐ χωρίζεται τῶν ἰδίων πατέρων, ἀλλὰ παραμένει αὐτοῖς ἄχρις ἐσχάτου γήρως, θεράπειαν αὐτοῖς ἀπονέμων [Philopatora boulomenoi sēmēnai anthrōpon, pelargon zōgraphousin; hypo gar tōn gennēsantōn ektrapheis ou chōrizetai tōn idiōn paterōn, alla paramenei autois achris eschatou gērōs, therapeian autois aponemōn]. When they wish to signify a son who loves his father, they paint a stork: for, having been reared by its parents, it is not separated from them, but stays with them right up to extreme old age, repaying them with care. Of the same kind is the fact that, to indicate that the force of justice lies beneath, ἐν τοῖς σκήπτροις ἀνωτέρω μὲν πελαργὸν τυποῦσι, κατωτέρω δὲ ποτάμιον ἵππον [en tois skēptrois anōterō men pelargon typousi, katōterō de potamion hippon], they carve a stork at the top of the sceptre and a hippopotamus at the bottom. So the Scholiast on Aristophanes on the Birds, and Suidas under the word Ἀντιπελαργεῖν [Antipelargein], which means to repay like with like, in the manner of storks; you may see it used in this sense everywhere by the ancients. Aristaenetus, book 1, Epistle 25: Οὕτω με νῦν ἀντιπελαργοῦσα δικαίαν ἀποδίδωσι χάριν [Houtō me nyn antipelargousa dikaian apodidōsi charin]. Basil, Hexaemeron, Homily 8: Τινὲς τῶν εὐεργετημάτων ἀντίδοσιν ἀντιπελάργωσιν ὀνομάζουσι [Tines tōn euergetēmatōn antidosin antipelargōsin onomazousi]. Ambrose, Hexaemeron [col. 328] book 5, chapter 16: The repayment of benefits is called ἀντιπελάργωσις [antipelargōsis]. Refer to the same point what is found in the Porta coeli, fol. 30d: ואומרים מין עוף אחד שנקרא ללא״ק שמפרנסין אביו ואמו אחר שיגדל כמו שפרנסו אותו בקטנותו, They say that there is a species of bird named lalak (read לקלאק laklak) which in turn feeds its parents when they have grown old, just as it was fed by them when little. But whoever wants more on this subject should read Basil and Ambrose in those passages, Philo on the Decalogue, Epiphanius in the Physiologus, chapter 25, Eustathius on the Hexaemeron, Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)], On Animals, chapter 6, and the paroemiographers Zenobius, Apostolius and Erasmus [=Desiderius Erasmus, Adagia], at the words Ἀντιπελαργεῖν [Antipelargein] and Πελαργικοὶ νόμοι [Pelargikoi nomoi]. For we have no leisure to dwell longer on a matter so utterly hackneyed. I add only that storks show their gratitude not only towards their parents but towards anyone else, if Aelian's ^{b)} story of the woman of Tarentum, Heracleis, is true. When she had bound up a stork's broken leg and brought it back to health with her remedies, the following year the stork, mindful of the kindness received, dropped into her lap a stone by whose brilliance the house shone at night, ὡς εἰσκομισθείσης δᾳδὸς [hōs eiskomistheisēs dados], as if a torch had been brought in. I understand this as the lychnis, or lychnites, by which houses are lit up at night as though by lighted lamps. See Lucian, On the Syrian Goddess, and Pliny, book 37, chapter 7, and, what is most to the point, Philostratus, in whom πελαργοὶ καλιὰς οὐκ ἂν πήξαιντο, μὴ πρότερον αὐταῖς ἐναρμόσαντες τὸν λυχνίτην λίθον [pelargoi kalias ouk an pēxainto, mē proteron autais enarmosantes ton lychnitēn lithon], storks never build nests [III, 87] without placing the lychnites stone in them. Goblerus, in Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], reports that something similar happened at Wesel. There, namely, a stork that used to nest every year on the same house, after experiencing the kindness of its host for many years, on returning from its usual migration around the beginning of spring, threw at his feet, as if in thanks, a green ginger root, as a guest-gift and token of hospitality. Moreover the stork is also extremely φιλόστοργος [philostorgos] towards its chicks, and, if food to nourish them is not available from elsewhere, then, like the pelican, as they say, τὴν ἑαυτοῦ χτιζὴν (τροφὴν) ἀνεμέσας ἐκείνους τρέφει [tēn heautou chtizēn (trophēn) anemesas ekeinous trephei], it feeds them by vomiting up yesterday's food. So Aelian in the passage cited above. From all this it becomes plain to the reader that the name חסידה hasida, as if you were to say kind and pious, suits the stork for many reasons ^{R1}.

The second proof is drawn from those passages of Scripture in which the hasida is treated. For in them whatever is attributed to the hasida fits the stork best. To make this plain to the reader, it is worth running through and examining all of them.

I. Moses counts the hasida among the unclean birds and forbids the Jews to eat it. This suits the stork exceedingly well, for it feeds on serpents and venomous animals, and in the nest it feeds its young on no other food. Juvenal, Satire 14:
— — the stork feeds its young on the serpent, and on the lizard found in the trackless fields.

Hence it was highly prized in Thessaly. Aristotle in the Marvels: Περὶ Θετταλίαν μνημονεύουσιν ὄφεις ζωογονηθῆναι τοσούτους, ὥστε. εἰ μὴ ὑπὸ τῶν πελαργῶν ἀνῃροῦντο, ἐκχωρῆσαι ἂν αὐτούς· [Peri Thettalian mnēmoneuousin opheis zōogonēthēnai tosoutous, hōste ei mē hypo tōn pelargōn anērounto, ekchōrēsai an autous] They say that around Thessaly so many serpents are bred that, were they not destroyed by the storks, the region would have to be abandoned. Plutarch in Isis: Θεσσαλοὶ δὲ πελαργοὺς (ἐτίμησαν), ὅτι, πολλοὺς ὄφεις τῆς γῆς ἀναδιδούσης, ἐπιφανέντες ἐξώλεσαν ἅπαντας· [Thessaloi de pelargous (etimēsan), hoti, pollous opheis tēs gēs anadidousēs, epiphanentes exōlesan hapantas] The Thessalians held storks in honour, because, when their land had produced many serpents, [III, 88] they destroyed them all by their arrival. Pliny, book 10, chapter 23: So great is the honour paid them for destroying serpents that in Thessaly it was a capital crime to have killed one. Solinus on Thessaly: Where there is an enormous quantity of serpents; by hunting them for food (the storks) remove a great deal of harm from the Thessalian districts. So too Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)] on Egypt: The Egyptians rightly [col. 329] love storks, both because of the frogs, which are born there in excessive abundance and which they consume, and because they even swallow serpents whole. Accordingly the Muslims still dispute today whether it is lawful to eat اللغلق [al-laghlaq] alleklek, that is, the stork. Some indeed permit it, كالكركي [ka-l-kurkī] like the crane: but most forbid it, بانه ياكل الحيات [bi-annahu yaʾkul al-ḥayyāt] because it eats serpents. Thus from the rule by which all water birds are permitted this bird alone is excepted, with a further reason added, that دف في طيرانه كما تفعل الجوارح [daffa fī ṭayarānihi kamā tafʿal al-jawāriḥ] it moves its wings in flight as if beating with them, as birds of prey do, all of which are forbidden. The theologians of that impure sect explain this at greater length in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]. That the leklek is the stork, not the crane, as many explain it in Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], is shown both by the description itself and by this statement of Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār]: فالرغوس هو اللغلق [fālarghūs huwa al-laghlaq] Πελαργὸς [Pelargos] is alleklek. It is also written with Gain, اللغلغ [al-laghlagh] allegleg, although in the Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] some would have لقلق [laqlaq] leklek and لغلغ [laghlagh] legleg be different birds; but wrongly, since no description anywhere exists of a bird لغلغ [laghlagh] legleg distinct from the stork. And Damir begins his treatise On the stork thus: اللغلق طاير طويل العنق وربما قالوا اللغلغ [al-laghlaq ṭāʾir ṭawīl al-ʿunuq wa-rubbamā qālū al-laghlagh] Alleklek, a long-necked bird, which they sometimes call allegleg. From both is compounded the Turkish name of the stork, leglek, in Gesner, for which one should read leklek or legleg. And it is wrongly called Turkish, since it is purely Arabic. The Turkish word, however, is tuigon, as Busbecq asserts in his Letters On the Turkish embassy ^{R2}.

II. The second passage on the hasida is Job 39:16 (var. 13.), where the ostrich is compared with the hasida, that is, with the stork, with respect to wing and plumage. For the Sacred Writer says: The wing of ostriches exults, truly a wing as of the stork, [III, 89] and plumage, that is, of the same colour as it. That this clause must be rendered so, we have shown with many arguments ^{c)} in the treatise On the ostrich; and the ostrich is rightly compared in this respect with the stork, because of the mixture of black with white in the colour of their feathers. Hence Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)], Against Cardano, Exercise 230: All (ostriches) are marked with dark and white, as many African merchants told me; and so that I might understand it better, they compared it to the colour of the stork. Marmol, on the ostrich, in his Africa, book 1, chapter 23: En las alas, y en la cola tiene grandes plumas negras, y blancas, comelas de cigueña, that is, On the wings and on the tail it has large black and white feathers, like the feathers of the stork. For there is no one who does not know that storks are marked with these colours. Hence Albertus: The stork has black wings, and a white tail and other parts. And Turner [=William Turner, Avium praecipuarum historia (1544)]: It is a bird of a size between the crane and the heron, marked with white and black feathers. Nor does the Greek name of the stork, πελαργὸς [pelargos], come from anywhere else; it is observed to be compounded of two opposites, namely black and white. For πελὸν [pelon] means τὸ μέλαν [to melan], καὶ ἀργὸν τὸ λευκόν [kai argon to leukon]. See Suidas, the Etymologicum and Eustathius on Iliad λ΄ [11]. From this mixture of colours the γυπαίετος [gypaietos], the vulture-eagle, is called ὀρειπέλαργος [oreipelargos], that is, mountain stork, and περκνόπτερος [perknopteros], that is, having black wings. See Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 32, and Pliny, book 10, chapter 3. And in Lycophron the πελαργοχρῶτες, αἱ Φαλακραίαι κόραι [pelargochrōtes, hai Phalakraiai korai], Phalacraean daughters having the colour of storks, are the ships of the Greeks built at Phalacra, a promontory of Ida, [col. 330] and having a mixed τὸ πελὸν καὶ τὸ ἀργὸν χρῶμα [to pelon kai to argon chrōma], black and white colour ^{R3}.

III. The third passage on the hasida is Psal. CIV, 17. (var. CIII, 19.) חסידה ברושים ביתה, The firs are the house of the hasida. Here house stands for nest, as in Psalm. [III, 90] LXXXIV, 4. (var. LXXXIII, 3.) Even the sparrow has found בית קן, a nest for itself. So in the second book of the Georgics,
And he tears up the ancient homes of the birds together with the lowest roots. — —
And in the Epigram the swallow
— — — — πηλοδομεῖ θάλαμον [pēlodomei thalamon],

builds itself a chamber of mud for a house, that is, constructs its nest with the greatest skill. Since the ancients, Aristotle, Pliny, Plutarch and Aelian, extol this skill of the swallow with so much praise, it is surprising that they kept such deep silence about the structure of the stork's nest, which shows no less industry in this respect. Hence Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] says of the leklek, or stork: فياتي بالاعواد والحشيش وتركب بعضها في بعض تركيبا عجيبا [fa-yaʾtī bi-l-aʿwād wa-l-ḥashīsh wa-tarkab baʿḍahā fī baʿḍ tarkīban ʿajīban] It brings sticks and grasses, which it fits together in a marvellous structure. And Caspar Heldelinus, in his Encomium Ciconiae, who treats the subject most carefully: Immediately upon its first arrival the stork returns to its old nest. If it finds it safe and intact, it at once cleans it of the filth gathered during the winter neglect and restores it; but if it sees that it has been thrown down by some fiercer storm of winds, it straightway carries in twigs from the fields and marsh sedge and takes possession of the site with a new nest. First it lays out round boundaries very like a sundial; soon it builds; then it makes it firm. Finally, if anything sticks out too crookedly, it puts it in order with a wonderful industry of its beak. Moreover, they mostly build their nest on the tops of towers or on the gables of houses. Yet this is not invariable, for there are some that prefer to live in the fields. Hence Varro, Res Rusticae, book 3, chapter 5: Migrant birds rear their young, storks in the field, swallows under the roof. The nest of the field stork is in the branches of trees. Hence Olympiodorus on Job: Οὐ γὰρ εἰς γῆν τίκτει ὁ πελαργὸς, ἀλλ᾽ εἰς τὰ ὑψηλὰ τῶν δένδρων· [Ou gar eis gēn tiktei ho pelargos, all᾽ eis ta hypsēla tōn dendrōn] For the stork lays its eggs not on the ground but in lofty trees. And Alkazuinius: ولا يتخذ الوكرا الا في موضع عال كمنارة وشجرة [wa-lā yattakhidh al-wakrā illā fī mawḍiʿ ʿāl ka-manāra wa-shajara] Nor does it take a nest for itself except in a high place, for instance on a lighthouse or in a tree. And Heldelinus: It nests on the higher gables of houses, or, more rarely, in dry trees nearby. This the stork has in common with the heron: though a water bird, it nests in high places. Gesner: Although the heron seeks its food in the waters, it places its nest in woods and tall trees. Polydore Vergil, Anglica Historia, book 1: The heron is accustomed afterwards to nest in crows' nests, that is, in the tops of trees, as he adds a little later. David, however, uses firs, and a little before the cedars of Lebanon, for any tall tree, just as he uses stork for any bird that nests in a tree. The cedars of Lebanon, (he says) which he [III, 91] planted, that the birds may nest there; and the house of the stork, the firs. Although I do not in the least doubt that storks are frequent on Lebanon itself, as on the other mountain of Syria, Amanus, of which Belon says: The storks which are in Europe in summer spend a large part of the winter, as in Egypt, so also around Antioch and near Mount Amanus.

IV. The fourth passage is Jer 8:7. Even the hasida in the heaven knows her times, that is, when she must migrate from one place to another, and what the time is for departing or returning. This fits the stork as well as the rest that has been adduced. [col. 331] For it is well known that the stork is a migratory bird. And the Philosopher is objected in vain, who says that it φωλεῖν [phōlein], that is, lies hidden: Φωλεῖ, he says, ^{d)} καὶ πελαργὸς, καὶ κόττυφος, καὶ τρυγὼν, καὶ κόρυδος [Phōlei kai pelargos, kai kottyphos, kai trygōn, kai korydos]. The stork too lies hidden, and the blackbird, and the turtledove, and the lark. For that the stork withdraws and migrates to other places is taught by four kinds of witnesses. I. Greek and Roman writers. Petronius, quoting Publius:
Exile of winter, herald of the warm season.

Pliny, book 10, chapter 23: From what place storks come, or where they betake themselves, is not yet known. That they come from far away is not in doubt, in the same manner as cranes. See the rest there. Solinus, chapter 40: Pythonos Come in Asia is a place of open plains, where at the time of their first arrival the storks fly together and tear to pieces the one that came last. (Just as Caesar reports that among the Gauls, whoever had come last to the council was customarily subjected to every kind of torture and put to death in the sight of the multitude.) Aelian, History, book 3, chapter 23: Προακούω δὲ τοὺς πελαργοὺς καὶ αὐταῖς συμφεύγειν ταῖς γεράνοις, καὶ συναποδιδράσκειν τὸν χειμῶνα· τῆς δὲ ὥρας τῆς κρυμώδους διελθούσης ὅταν ὑποστρέφωσιν εἰς τὰ ἴδια, καὶ οἵδε καὶ αἵδε, τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστος καλιὰν ἀναγνωρίζουσιν, ὡς τὴν οἰκίαν ἄνθρωποι [Proakouō de tous pelargous kai autais sympheugein tais geranois, kai synapodidraskein ton cheimōna; tēs de hōras tēs krymōdous dielthousēs hotan hypostrephōsin eis ta idia, kai hoide kai haide, tēn heautōn hekastos kalian anagnōrizousin, hōs tēn oikian anthrōpoi]. I also hear that storks flee with the cranes and depart together with them in winter; and that, when the cold is over, both these and those, migrating back to their native abode, each recognize their own nests as men recognize their home. Accordingly they hold that the Pelasgians, διὰ τὸ πλανήτας εἶναι, καὶ δίκην ὀρνέων ἐπιφοιτᾷν ἐφ᾽ οὓς ἔτυχε τόπους, Πελαργοὺς ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀττικῶν κληθῆναι [dia to planētas einai, kai dikēn orneōn epiphoitan eph' hous etyche topous, Pelargous hypo tōn Attikōn klēthēnai], because they were wanderers and roamed into any places whatever like storks, were called Pelargoi by the Athenians. So Strabo in book 5; and again in book 9: Ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀττικῶν Πελαργοὶ προσηγορεύθησαν διὰ τὴν πλάνην [Hypo tōn Attikōn Pelargoi prosēgoreuthēsan dia tēn planēn], On account of their wanderings they were called Pelargoi by the Athenians. (Although in the Etymologicum some prefer that they were so called διὰ τὰς σινδόνας, ἃς ἐφόρουν [dia tas sindonas, has ephoroun], on account of the garments they wore, marked like storks with black and [III, 92] white.) II. Many of the Fathers assert the same of storks. Thus Basil writes in Homily 8: Κατὰ τὸν ἕνα καιρὸν πάντας ἐπιδημεῖν τοῖς τῇ δε χωρίοις, οὕτω δὲ ὑφ᾽ ἑνὶ συνθήματι πάντας ἀπαίρειν [Kata ton hena kairon pantas epidēmein tois tē de chōriois, houtō de hyph' heni synthēmati pantas apairein], All make for these places at one time, and likewise all depart as if at one given signal. Which Eustathius imitates thus in the Hexaëmeron: Οἱ δὲ πελαργοὶ καὶ ἑνὶ ἐπιδημοῦσι συνθήματι, καὶ ἑνὶ ἀπαίρουσι [Hoi de pelargoi kai heni epidēmousi synthēmati, kai heni apairousi]. And Ambrose: They say that storks set out in a gathered troop, if they think they must go anywhere, and arrive together in many places around the East, and all move in unison as if at a military watchword. And Isidore: These heralds of spring, companions in fellowship, enemies of serpents, fly across the seas and proceed to Asia in a gathered troop. III. The Arabs and Hebrews too. Alkazuinius: لا يزال يتبع الربيع وله وكران احدهما بالجروم والاخر بالصرود ولا يزال يتحول من احدهما الي الاخر [lā yazālu yatbaʿu al-rabīʿ wa-lahu wakrān aḥaduhumā bi-l-jurūm wa-l-ākhar bi-l-ṣurūd wa-lā yazālu yataḥawwalu min aḥadihimā ilā al-ākhar] It never ceases to follow the spring; and, since it has two nests, one for summer and the other for winter, it does not cease to migrate from the one to the other. Damir from Avicenna: من ذكاه انه يتخذ له عشين يسكن في واحد منهما بعض وانه اذا احسن يتغير الهوا [min dhakāhu annahu yattakhidhu lahu ʿushshayn yaskunu fī wāḥid minhumā baʿḍ wa-annahu idhā aḥsana yataghayyaru al-hawā] It belongs to its cleverness that it has two nests, in one of which it dwells for some (supply الزمان [al-zamān] time, that is, for a while) and, when it is convenient, it changes air. Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] on Jeremiah: החסידה מנהגה לשכון [col. 332] בימי הקור והחורף במקום אחר ובימי הקיץ והחום במקום אחר, In the time of cold and winter the stork is wont to dwell in one place, and in another in the days of summer and heat. IV. More recent writers. Caspar Heldelinus: On the Ides of August the storks, young and old, in a most beautiful gathered troop, enter upon that laborious journey by night under the moon. But before they cross the sea, all those that our fields have sent forth gather at the Athesis, a river of Gaul, not very far from the Sextinian waters (for Sextinianis read Sextiis), or, as others prefer, the Sestian altars, namely where Marius routed the Cimbri with the sword. There, holding public assemblies among themselves, they murmur together, review the army, etc. Moreover, when about to depart, they prudently wait for a favourable north wind; and as soon as it blows more steadily, then, as if on a day fixed by law, they hasten their departure. Belon: When I was near Abydos, on 24 August, I saw a huge multitude of storks, which seemed to come to three or four thousand. They were flying from Russia and Tartary, and were crossing the Hellespont transversely in a crisscross formation. And when they were above Tenedos, they wheeled about in a long winding course until they were all gathered into a circle. Then, before going farther from the mouth of the Propontis, they divided themselves into some smaller squadrons, more than twenty, and followed one another toward the South. Since, therefore, storks depart and return at fixed times, the Prophet rightly said: The stork [III, 93] in the heaven knoweth her times. Kimchi understands by the stork in the heaven the stork that nests in a high place, בישוב במגדלי הגבוהים ובמדבר בעצים הגבוהים, namely on the highest towers, if the places are inhabited; or in the loftiest trees, if they are deserted; as it is said in the Psalm, The firs are her house. So Deut 1:28 and IX, 1.: Cities great and fortified בשמים, in heaven, that is, up to heaven. And Prov 30:19: The way of an eagle in the heaven, that is, which flies upward. Yet, since the stork's nest is not in question here, I prefer to interpret thus: the stork in the heaven, that is, in the air, and from the air, knows the time of its migration, and that it must depart when the air grows warm and the cold abates.

V. The last passage is Zechariah, chapter 5, verse 9, where the Prophet sees in a prophetic vision two women flying between heaven and earth, ורוח בכנפיהם ולהנה כנפים ככנפי החסידה, who had wind in their wings, and their wings were like the wings of the hasida, that is, of the stork. For why should I not translate it so? I do not now inquire what those two women signify, because the matter is full of obscurities and not necessary in this place. I assert only that by wings full of wind are meant here wings supremely well equipped for flight. Such are the wings of storks, with which they migrate to and return from very remote places, though places not well enough known. Pliny ^{e)}: From what place they come, or where they betake themselves, is still undiscovered. That they come from far away is not in doubt. Oppian in the Ixeutica: Whence they come and whither they return is not well established. Some say they fly from Lycia, others from Ethiopia. This seems capable of confirmation from the story we touched on above ^{f)} about a ginger root, still fresh, brought into Germany by a stork. For ginger grows mostly in Ethiopia, or, what is the same, Troglodytic Arabia. Dioscorides, book 1: Ζιγγίβερις ἴδιόν ἐστι φυτὸν, γεννώμενον ἐν τῇ Τρωγλοδυτικῇ Ἀραβίᾳ πλεῖστον [Zingiberis idion esti phyton, gennōmenon en tē Trōglodytikē Arabia pleiston]. Pliny, book 12, chapter 7, on pepper: The root of this tree is not, as some have supposed, what they call zimpiberi, and others zingiberi, although it is similar in taste. For that grows in Arabia and Troglodytica, on farms. Nor did Galen mean anything else when he wrote in book 6 of the Simples that ginger is imported from Barbaria. For Ethiopian Barbaria is meant, of which we spoke above ^{g)}. It must be admitted, meanwhile, that various places of India, such as Malabar, Bengala, Babul, Becain, are productive of ginger, as travellers testify, and that it is also found in the Omanitis of [col. 333] Arabia Felix. For so Abuchanipha: زنجبيل هو مما ينبت في بلاد العرب في الارض عمان [zanjabīl huwa mimmā yanbutu fī bilād al-ʿarab fī al-arḍ ʿumān] Ginger is among the things that grow in Arabia, in the land of Oman. But wherever ginger grows, from there to Germany [III, 94] is an immense journey, with much sea lying between, which storks would not cross unless they were exceedingly strong of wing ^{R4}.

Having thus examined the passages of Scripture, the third argument by which we have proved that the hasida is the stork rests on the authority of many interpreters. For although we have shown by a long enumeration that most have gone astray, there still remain many for whom the hasida is the stork. Among these are, 1., those of the Greeks whom Olympiodorus refutes with worthless reasons: The stork, he says, does not lay its eggs on the ground. But neither does the ἀσίδα [asida], as he would have it, deceived by the version of the Greeks, who seem to attribute to the asida what the Hebrew text attributes to the ostrich. Nor is what he adds of greater weight, that τοὺς ὀρνιθιακὰ γράψαντας [tous ornithiaka grapsantas] distinguished the asida from the stork. For the Greek and Roman writers who treated of birds have nothing about the name asida, because it is Hebrew, not Greek or Latin. The others before Olympiodorus I do not regard, most of whom were entirely ignorant both of Hebrew and of the nature of birds. 2. To the Greeks we add the Syrians, for whom the hasida is ܚܘܪܒܐ [חורבא] hurba. So they render it everywhere, except in the passage of Job. Moreover, for the most learned of the Maronites ܚܘܪܒܐ [חורבא] is the stork ^{R5}. 3. To these are added the Arabic translators of the Prophets, who in Ierem. VIII, 7. and Zachar. V, 9. have for hasida القعقع [al-qaʿqaʿ] alkoko, that is, the stork, not the crane, as Gabriel would have it, much less the magpie. For although القعقع [al-qaʿqaʿ] alkoko sometimes means the magpie, it also means the stork, and the matter requires that it be taken so here. Alcamus: القعقع العقعق وطاير اخر ابلق بري [al-qaʿqaʿ al-ʿaqʿaq wa-ṭāyir ākhar ablaq barrī] [III, 95] طويل المنقار والرجلين [ṭawīl al-minqār wa-al-rijlayn] Alkoko, the magpie, and another bird, pied, of the wild, with a long beak and legs. Damir, in one copy: القعقع طاير ابلق من طير الما طويل المنقار قاله الجوهري وابن سيدة وزاد وفيه بياض وسواد [al-qaʿqaʿ ṭāyir ablaq min ṭayr al-mā ṭawīl al-minqār qālahu al-Jawharī wa-Ibn Sīda wa-zāda wa-fīhi bayāḍ wa-sawād] Alkoko, a pied bird of the water birds, with a long beak. So Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ] and Ibno-Saida assert; the latter of whom adds that this bird is marked with black and white. And in the other copy more explicitly: القعقع كلغلغ طاير ابلق ضخم من طير الما [al-qaʿqaʿ ka-laghlagh ṭāyir ablaq ḍakhm min ṭayr al-mā] Alkoko, the same as legleg (that is, the stork), a pied, bulky bird of the aquatic kind. So this is certain: that like some of the Greeks and the Syrians, so also some of the Arabs took the hasida for the stork ^{R6}. 4. Nor do the more recent Hebrews of the last six hundred years render it otherwise. [col. 334] See especially R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] on the Law; the same, and Kimchi, on Jeremiah; and Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] in his Lexicon. Accordingly, in the book entitled Masal Kadmoni, Fable 62, the speakers are הצפרדע והחסידה, that is, the frog and the stork, as appears from the picture. 5. Finally, the same is followed by the modern translators, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Munster, Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], Piscator, the English, Dutch, Italians, French, etc., and among the lexicographers, Santes, Schindler, Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum], etc. 6. Nor are there lacking those for whom the דיה לבנה of the Talmudists is not the kite or a white vulture, but πελαργὸς [pelargos], the stork: because, as דיה is formed from blackness and לבנה from whiteness, so the word πελαργὸς [pelargos] signifies a bird marked with white and black, as ^{h)} we have said. See Fuller [=Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea theologica / sacra (1612–22)], Miscellanea, book 6, chapter 10.

Now, if you compare this version with the rest, you will find it by far the best. For in all the others the fault is manifest. Thus in the heron, the coot, the swan, the kite and the ostrich there is nothing for which they should be named from piety. And, if you except the kite, none of them is migratory. The same judgement applies to the hoopoe. Nor do the coot, the swan and the ostrich nest in trees. And, however well the rest might fit, when one comes to the passage of Job, where the plumage of the hasida is compared with the feathers of the ostrich, I see no bird other than the stork to which this could apply [III, 96] ^{R7}. These things we offer by way of example. For anyone who undertakes a comparison of the passages on the hasida will supply the rest for himself.

It remains to add a few remarks on the various names of storks. The Hebrew חסידה hasida and the Greek πελαργὸς [pelargos] have already been fully explained. The Syriac ܚܘܪܒܐ [חורבא] hurba seems to have been formed by metathesis from ܚܘܒܪܐ [חוברא] hubra, which would mean the sociable bird. Of the Israelites it is said in Iud. XX, 11.: All the Israelites were gathered together, as one man, חברים, companions. See the same thing in Pliny about storks! When about to depart they gather in a fixed place, and they keep together in such a way that none of their kind is left behind, unless it is captive and enslaved. The Arabic لقلق [laqlaq] leklek and لغلغ [laghlagh] legleg were formed from the stork's cry, as the Arabs expressly teach. Damir: وصوته اللقلقه وكذلك كل صوت فيه حركه واضطراب [wa-ṣawtuhu al-laqlaqa wa-kadhālika kull ṣawt fīhi ḥaraka wa-iḍṭirāb] And laklaka is the cry of the stork, and every sound that is produced with vibration and agitation. Accordingly laklaka is also the name for the hiss of a serpent, produced with the tongue thrust out. Moreover, this cry of the stork does not come from deep in the throat, but is made by the two parts of the bill striking against each other, like a castanet or a rattle. Hence Publilius Syrus calls it crotalistria [castanet-player], and Ovid, in book 6 of the Metamorphoses, says
— — the stork with rattling bill.

And Solinus wrote that the sound with which they rattle is of the mouth rather than of the voice. But he would have done better to say of the bill. Philostratus too, in his Letter to Epictetus: Καὶ τοὺς πελαργοὺς, ἐπειδὰν παριόντας ἡμᾶς κροτῶσιν [Kai tous pelargous, epeidan pariontas hēmas krotōsin], that is, The storks, when they rattle at us as we pass by. For the word there is κροτῶσιν [krotōsin], whence crotalistria. The Latin name CICONIA also goes back to the same thing. Isidore: Storks (CICONIAE) are so called, as if cicaniae, from the sound with which they rattle, which they make by shaking the bill. Nor is there any doubt that the Arabic العقعق [al-ʿaqʿaq] alkoko, which we explained above ^{i)}, alludes to this very thing.

notes.text: But to this argument, which is drawn from the etymology, Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] in the Supplemm. vol. 3, p. 857 attributes little or nothing. "The name," he says, "can be derived from piety for several birds, and has been so derived, as for the vulture רחם from mercy, and for others, also here and there for חסידה; nor is this the only etymology offered by the oriental languages. For the חסידה, still unknown to us, could also be called from ܚܣܕܐ [חסדא], disgrace, a foul bird; from the Arabic حسد [ḥasad], envious; from a marsh and a confluence of water [Michaelis no doubt has in view the Arabic حشد [ḥashada] he gathered, flowed together], marshy, dwelling in marshes. The lack of an etymology may be urged against some interpretations; none can be established by an etymology." So Michaelis, and rightly, as it seems to me. To this I add that piety is also celebrated in the heron, or herodius (see Aelian, Hist. Anim. book 3, ch. 23), the bird which the most ancient translators took for the Hebrew חסידה, as we saw in the preceding Chapter. Their interpretation can therefore be confirmed by this same etymology.
notes.label: R1

notes.text: What Bochart adduces in the first place to prove that חסידה is the stork is this: Moses counts the chasida among the unclean birds and forbids the Jews to eat it, and this fits the stork especially well, since it feeds on serpents. But this reason for the prohibition fits many birds of the heron kind, which have this in common, that they feed on fish, frogs, serpents and aquatic insects. This argument, then, being too general, proves nothing.
notes.label: R2

notes.text: This mixture of black and white in the colour of the feathers, too, the stork shares with many birds of the heron kind. Thus Aldrovandi [=Ulisse Aldrovandi, Ornithologia (1599–1603)], Ornithol. vol. 3, p. 377 f., on the Ardea cinerea, or the herodius of the ancients: "The upper neck, the whole back, likewise the wings, except the larger feathers, and also the tail are of an ash-grey colour. The flight feathers of the wings are blackish. The belly is white, as are also the breast and the lower neck, which are crossed by certain oblong black spots running downwards." The same on the second ash-grey heron, or the lesser, p. 380: "Among the black feathers of the crown others spring up that are white — — The wings are of a very handsome ash-grey colour, as is also the tail. But the neck in front and behind, the belly, the thighs and the underside of the tail are white." The same on the third kind of ash-grey heron, p. 383: "The feathers of the head, neck, back and upper wings are dusky from ash-grey, all marked at the tip with a reddish spot; those on the wings, which are rather larger, are variegated with white at the end, as are those that make up the tail. Those covering the breast are sprinkled with longer black, reddish and white markings. The belly is nearly white from ash-grey." You see, then, that this mark too is not so peculiar to the stork that another bird could not be thought of.
notes.label: R3

notes.text: But this whole argument, which Bochart adduced in the second place, is just as uncertain as the one he put first. Of the first and second marks we have already seen that they are found in more than one bird of the heron kind. But the rest too, everything attributed to the bird חסידה in the Sacred codex, fits the ardea cinerea, or the ἐρωδιός [erōdios] of the Alexandrian translator, each and every point, no less than the stork. For both birds nest in trees (Ps 104:17), both are migratory (Jer 8:7), and both, because of the swiftness of their flight, could be used as an image of the greatest speed (Zech 5:9). Cf. Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde], Vermischte Sammlungen, fasc. 5, ch. 6, p. 64 ff., and Michaelis, Supplemm. vol. 3, p. 859, 860.
notes.label: R4

notes.text: But Michaelis rightly warns, on Castell's [=Edmund Castell, Lexicon heptaglotton (London 1669)] Lexic. Syriac., edited by him, p. 320, and in the Supplemm. p. 859, that this authority of the most learned Maronites (who translated the Syriac version in the Polyglots into Latin) is nil; for they were accustomed to put under Syriac names of animals, trees and plants whose meanings they did not know the meanings that the common lexicons of their time gave for the Hebrew ones. Michaelis himself thinks it probable that the Syriac ܚܘܪܒܐ [חורבא] agrees with the Arabic خَرْبٌ [kharb], which Golius [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)] explains thus: the male of that bird whose whole kind is called حباري [ḥubārā], Hubara; which, as we saw above, is a species of otis or bustard.
notes.label: R5

notes.text: Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 3, p. 858: „I do not deny it, especially since I learn from the travels of Ives that the stork is called Legleg by the Arabs. But what does this Arab, the translator of the prophets, matter here, who translated not the Hebrew but the Greek, in which at Zech 5:9 the name ἔποπος [epopos], of the hoopoe, is read? This could certainly have been called قعقع [qaʿqaʿ] in Arabic from the variety of its colour. In Jeremiah, indeed, Ἀσιδα [Asida] now stands; but since the translator renders it in the same way as in Zechariah, he seems also to have read the same. Be that as it may, the Arabic translator of the prophets is neither of such an age, nor of such skill in Hebrew letters, which he did not even read, that any authority resides in him.“
notes.label: R6

notes.text: Yet we think we have sufficiently proved in the Notes to this chapter that all these things also fit the grey heron; hence I am in doubt between the stork and the grey heron. Oedmann, however, is certain that the Hebrews' חסידה is the grey heron, and Michaelis too inclines to this opinion, in Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] Hebrr. vol. III, p. 861: To one comparing everything, he says, formerly the kite seemed more probable, which I also expressed in the German version; now the heron,
notes.label: R7
